unit.title: Perform internal and external customer service

summary: This unit is about serving the people who rely on your work: clients and the public outside the firm, and the stores, office, estimator and other teams inside it. As a Level 3 electrician who leads a small team, you will learn to find out what a client really needs, explain technical matters in plain words, keep your promises, refuse unsafe requests without losing the client, handle complaints, hand over finished work, and set and measure service standards with your team.

blocks.p: This unit is for Level 3 electricians who lead a small team on installation and maintenance jobs and who speak to clients for the firm. Safe, neat work is the heart of the trade, but clients also judge the firm by how they are treated: whether you arrived when you said, listened to them, explained things clearly, kept their home clean and dealt fairly with problems. Most of that is in your hands as team leader.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Identify internal and external customers
Name who relies on your work inside the firm (stores, office, estimator, supervisor, other teams, apprentices) and outside it (home owners, businesses, the public), and say what each needs from you.
Find out what a client needs
Arrive prepared, ask open questions, listen actively, look at the installation, repeat the needs back and write them down.
Explain and advise in plain words
Explain faults, choices, costs and risks so the client can decide, without trade jargon and without scaring them.
Make realistic promises and keep them
Give dates and prices you can keep, put them in writing, and tell the client early when something changes.
Deal with unsafe or dishonest requests
Refuse politely, explain the danger, offer a safe choice with a price, and record your advice.
Serve every client fairly
Change the way you communicate to suit the person, respect their home, beliefs and privacy, and keep their keys, codes and details confidential.
Handle complaints
Listen, apologise, get the facts, make safe, agree a fix, escalate what is beyond your authority, follow up and remove the cause.
Hand over finished work
Show the client how to use the installation safely and hand over the certificate, circuit chart, manuals and warranty details.
Serve internal customers
Give the store, the office, the estimator and other trades what they need, correctly and on time.
Set and measure service standards
Agree clear standards, collect feedback, work out simple measures such as percentages, and lead the team to improve.

blocks.p: At Level 2 you served the client mainly by doing good work under supervision. At Level 3 you often **speak for the firm**: you may run the first visit, explain a quotation, deal with a complaint on site and lead a team whose behaviour the client sees every day. You also set the example. If you arrive late, leave a mess or talk about a client behind their back, your team will copy you.

blocks.note: In Jamaica a great deal of electrical work comes by word of mouth. A client who is well served tells family, church and workmates; one who is badly served tells even more people, and may post it online. Your service is the firm's advertising.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow a job from the first phone call to the follow-up after handover. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will add the Centre's own forms, such as the needs record, complaint log and feedback card.

A **customer** is anyone who relies on your work. **External customers** are outside the firm: they pay for or use its services. **Internal customers** are inside the firm: they need something from you so that they can do their own job.

head: Kind
Examples
What they need from you
rows: External customers
Home owners and tenants
Owners and managers of shops, hotels, clinics, schools and churches
Property managers and landlords
A main contractor, when your firm is a subcontractor
Members of the public near the work
Safe, tidy work; clear prices and dates; good manners; honest advice; work done when promised; problems put right.
Internal customers
The stores clerk
The office and accounts staff
The estimator
Your supervisor or manager
Other teams who share vans, tools and instruments
Apprentices in your own team
Correct information and paperwork on time; clear requests; equipment returned in good order; early warning of problems; respect.
Others you work with on a job
Other trades: plumbers, A/C installers, ceiling fixers, painters
The electrical inspector
JPS staff
They do not pay the firm, but the job depends on good relations: keep to agreed times, share your programme, keep your area tidy and be courteous.

blocks.p: If another trade asks your team to move a cable that is in their way, agree the best solution with them and your supervisor. If it must move, your team moves it, after safe isolation; never let another trade move electrical cables.
Service to the client is the last link in a chain of internal service. A typical chain looks like this:

flow: The client phones; the office records the details and books a visit
The team leader surveys the job and passes measurements and notes to the estimator
The estimator prices the job; the office sends the quotation
The store prepares materials from the team's written request
The team does the work, tests it and hands in the job card and test results
The office bills the client and the paperwork for the certificate is completed

blocks.p: If any link is weak, the client feels it. Missing measurements mean a wrong or late price. A vague material request means the wrong cable and a second trip. Late test results mean a late certificate and a client chasing the office.

head: Internal customer
Good service from your team
What poor service causes
rows: Stores clerk
Written requests with size, type, quantity and job number, sent before the agreed cut-off time; unused materials returned and booked back in; damaged tools reported.
Wrong or late materials, extra trips, lost stock, wasted money.
Office and accounts
Job cards, timesheets, variation forms and test results complete and handed in on time; the client's details correct.
Late or wrong bills, cash-flow problems, certificates held up, clients chasing.
Estimator
Survey sheets with route lengths, photos, the board and supply details and anything unusual.
Prices too low (the firm loses money) or too high (the firm loses the job), or quotations sent back and delayed.
Supervisor or manager
Early, honest warning of delays, problems and complaints.
Problems found too late to put right cheaply.
Other teams
Vans, tools and test instruments returned clean, charged and complete.
The next team starts late or uses faulty equipment.
Apprentices in your team
Clear instructions, safe tasks, time to learn and respect.
Mistakes, accidents, poor work and trainees who give up.

blocks.p: Many firms write short agreements between departments so that each side knows what to expect. For example: 'Written material requests received by 3 p.m. are packed for collection at 7 a.m. the next working day' and 'Test results reach the office within one working day of the test.' An agreement like this is a service standard for internal customers.

blocks.note: Treat internal customers with the same courtesy as clients. The stores clerk who is hurried and shouted at on Monday is not keen to stay late for you on Friday.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Finding out what the client needs

ul: Answer the phone with the firm's name and your own name.
Take the client's name, the address with a landmark, a phone number, what the problem or job is and how urgent it is.

If there is danger now, such as burning smells, sparking or a shock from an appliance, tell the client to switch off at the main breaker if it is safe to do so, keep people away and call the firm back or call 110 in an emergency.
Give a visit time you can keep, confirm it by message, and say who will come.
If a client phones while you are doing something risky, such as working on a roof or at an open panel, finish the step safely and get to a safe place first, then call back promptly.
Arrive on time. If you will be late, call before the agreed time, not after.
Wear a clean uniform and carry the firm's ID. Introduce yourself and your team.
Ask permission before you go into rooms, move furniture or open cupboards.
Respect the property: use dust sheets, wipe your boots, and do not use the client's things without asking.
Put your phone away while the client is talking to you.

head: Question type
Example
Use it to
rows: Open (what, how, why, tell me about)
'How do you use this room during the day?'
Get the client to explain in their own words, and find needs you had not thought of.
Closed (yes/no or one fact)
'Is the water heater on its own breaker?'
Confirm a fact quickly.
Probing (follow-up)
'You said the lights dim. When exactly does that happen?'
Dig deeper into an answer.
Checking (summary)
'So you want four more outlets and the porch light on a timer. Is that right?'
Make sure you have understood before you leave.

blocks.p: Start with open questions to learn about the client's situation, then use closed questions to pin down the details. A fault call is the same: 'Which breaker trips, and what is switched on when it does?' tells you far more than 'Does it trip often?'

ul: Look at the client, nod and let them finish. Do not plan your reply while they are still talking.
Take notes, and say that you are doing so.
Ask follow-up questions about anything unclear.
**Repeat the main points back in your own words** (paraphrase). This shows you have understood, and lets the client correct you.
Watch the client's face and tone: a worried look when you mention cost may mean the budget matters more than they have said.

blocks.p: A client tells you what they want: this is the **stated need**. Behind it there is often a need they do not mention: the **unstated need**. Good service meets both.

head: The client says
The need behind it
What you might suggest
rows: 'I want an outlet beside my mother's bed.'
Her oxygen concentrator must keep running.
A dedicated circuit, and advice on a backup supply (a UPS, or a generator with a proper changeover switch).
'The lights keep flickering.'
To know that the house is safe.
Find the cause, such as a loose connection, before changing any lamps.
'I need more outlets in the shop.'
To run more equipment without breakers tripping.
A load check, and new circuits where needed instead of power strips.
'Make the yard brighter.'
Security at night.
Dusk-to-dawn or motion-sensor LED floodlights aimed at the gate and doors.
'I want more light in the restaurant.'
The right mood for diners, within a budget.
Find out how the room is used and the feel wanted, then offer dimmable or zoned lighting.

blocks.h: The first visit, step by step

flow: Greet, introduce yourself and show your ID
Ask open questions about what is wanted and why, the budget and the timing
Walk through each area with the client and note what is wanted where
Check the board, the supply (110 V / 220 V), the grounding and any signs of overheating
Ask about other work planned, such as A/C units, solar or renovations
Repeat the needs back and write them on the needs record
Explain what happens next and when, and thank the client

blocks.p: Write down the client's details, what they want room by room, measurements and photos, the board and supply details, access (working hours, keys, pets, occupants), the budget, who makes the decisions and who pays, and the next step you promised. Read it back to the client. Copies go to the estimator and the office, so the people who price and plan the job work from the same facts. Write any special request (a room to keep locked, where to park, a day to avoid) on the job card and brief the team, so the people who do the work know it too.

blocks.note: If you are unsure about anything on the first visit, ask then. A two-minute question can save a second trip, a wrong price or a day of rework.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Explaining technical matters in plain words

ul: Start with what it means for the client: safety, cost, comfort or time.
Use everyday words. Explain any trade word you cannot avoid.
Compare with something familiar, show the faulty part or a photo, or draw a quick sketch.
Give the choices, with the cost and the advantages and drawbacks of each.
Do not scare the client or exaggerate the danger to win the work, and never make them feel foolish.
Check understanding: invite questions, and ask what they would like to do next.
If a client does not understand a quotation or an invoice, go through it line by line and answer each question.

head: Trade term
Plain words for a client
rows: Overload
Too many things running on one circuit, so the cable gets too hot.
Short circuit
Two wires touching, so a huge current flows and the breaker switches off at once.
Ground (earth) fault
Electricity escaping to metal parts or the ground, which could give someone a shock.
Equipment grounding conductor
The safety wire that carries a fault away so the breaker trips, instead of the metal case of an appliance staying live.
GFCI
A special outlet or breaker that switches off very fast if electricity leaks through a person.
Insulation breakdown
The plastic coating on old wires has gone hard and cracked, so bare metal can touch.
Voltage drop
Power lost along a long cable, so equipment at the far end gets less than it should.

blocks.p: **Example.** 'The safety wire to your kitchen outlets is broken. Right now, if the kettle developed a fault, its metal body could stay live and give someone a shock instead of tripping the breaker. We need to replace that cable. It is about half a day's work and costs J$… . Until then, please do not use those outlets.'

Give the facts, then let the client decide. For lighting, for example, explain what each choice costs to buy, what it costs to run and how long it lasts. Tell the truth about savings: a rough figure you can show is better than a big promise you cannot. Recommend what suits the client's needs and budget, not what earns the firm most. Never accept a payment from a supplier for recommending a product.

Visitors and clients with imported equipment need special advice. JPS supplies **110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz**. Equipment from North America is usually made for 120 V or 240 V at **60 Hz**. Before anything is plugged in, check its rating plate for the voltage and the frequency, and explain what you find.

head: Part of a quotation
Why it matters
rows: Client's name, site address, date and quotation number
Identifies the job.
Description of the work (the scope)
Says exactly what is included, so both sides agree what is being bought.
Exclusions
Says what is **not** included, such as patching and painting walls, builder's work, equipment the client supplies, or fees paid by the client. This prevents arguments later.
Price before GCT, GCT at the current rate on its own line, and the total
Clear and honest; no surprise at the end.
Time on site and expected start date
Sets the client's expectations.
How long the price is valid (for example 30 days)
Material prices change.
Payment terms
Deposit and stage payments agreed in advance.
Warranty
What is covered and for how long.
Acceptance (signature)
Shows the client has agreed.

ul: **Promise only what you can keep.** Allow for delivery times, the inspection, rain, other trades and the client's own hours.
If you are unsure, give a range ('Tuesday or Wednesday') and confirm the day as soon as you know.
Put dates and prices in writing.
When the client asks for a change, explain its effect on cost and time and get it agreed in writing **before** you do it (a variation).
It is better to promise Thursday and arrive on Wednesday than to promise Monday and arrive on Thursday.

blocks.h: When a promise cannot be kept

flow: Find out as soon as possible that the date or price will change
Tell the client before the promised date, not after it has passed
Apologise and explain the reason honestly
Offer a new date or price, and anything that reduces the trouble, such as doing part of the work first
Confirm the new arrangement in writing
Keep the new promise

blocks.note: A client may have taken a day off work, emptied a shop or planned money around your price. A broken promise costs them, not just you. An early, honest call keeps most clients' trust; silence loses it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Sooner or later a client will ask you to do something unsafe, against the wiring code or dishonest, usually to save money or time. You must refuse. How you refuse decides whether you keep the client.

head: Request
Why you must refuse
Safe choice to offer
rows: Connect a portable generator with a cord that has a plug on each end, into a dryer or other outlet

The pins of the free plug are live. If the main is on, the generator feeds back through the meter into JPS lines and can kill a line worker who thinks the line is dead. It can also damage the generator when JPS power returns.
A changeover (transfer) switch or approved interlock, installed and inspected, so the house is fed from JPS or the generator, never both.
Fit a bigger breaker because a circuit keeps tripping
The breaker protects the cable. A bigger one lets the cable overheat and can start a fire.
Find out why it trips; move some load to another circuit; add a new circuit.
Run a new A/C unit from an extension cord
The cord and outlet are not rated for the load and can overheat and burn.
A dedicated circuit of the right size, as the A/C maker requires.
Take out the bathroom GFCI because it keeps tripping
It is the device that protects people in wet places. Tripping means current is leaking somewhere.
Find and repair the leaking appliance or wiring.
Switch on before the testing is finished, because of a party tonight
Untested circuits may have faults that cause shock or fire.
Explain that nothing is energised until it is tested; offer the earliest safe time, or a properly tested temporary supply.
Bury junction boxes behind plaster or in a sealed ceiling
Connections must stay accessible for checking and repair; hidden joints can overheat unseen.
Accessible boxes with covers, placed where they can be reached.
Connect to a neighbour's supply or bypass the meter
It is illegal and dangerous.
Apply to JPS for a supply in the proper way.

blocks.h: How to refuse and keep the client

flow: Listen and show you understand the reason, such as cost or time
Explain the danger in plain words
Say clearly that you cannot do it, and why: people's safety, the code and the firm's rules
Offer safe choices, each with a price
Put your advice in writing; if the client still insists, tell your supervisor and record it

blocks.note: A client's signature does not make unsafe work safe. Nobody can sign away the safety of their family, their neighbours or a JPS line worker, and you remain responsible for the work you do.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Do not take private 'side jobs' from the firm's clients or do work 'off the books' for cash. Decline politely and refer the work to the firm.
Follow the firm's rules on gifts. Tell your supervisor about anything more than a small token.
Never overstate a fault to sell more work. Charge only for work done and materials used.
Admit mistakes and put them right.
Anything you find on a client's premises, such as cash or jewellery in a ceiling, belongs to the client. Stop, call a witness, hand it over against a signature and record it.
Keys, alarm codes and gate remotes are logged out and in, kept locked away and returned promptly.
Do not talk about clients' homes, possessions, routines or problems to other people or on social media.
Take photos only of what the job needs, and ask first in private areas.
Use clients' personal details only for the job. Jamaica's data protection law requires firms to keep personal information secure and to use it only for the purpose it was given.
If someone you do not know asks about a client's installation or security, give no information. Refer them to the client.

blocks.h: Keeping the client and the public safe

ul: Tell the occupants which areas are unsafe while you work, and put up barriers and signs.
Keep children and pets away; ask the client to secure dogs before you start.
Lock tools and materials away; never leave cut cable ends or open boxes where people can reach them.
Tell the client when the power will be off, and for how long, so fridges, computers and medical equipment can be planned for.
Clean up at the end of each day.

blocks.p: Every client gets the **same standard of service**, whatever their age, background, religion, gender, disability, accent or how much money they have. What changes is **how you communicate**, not the quality of the work or the respect you show.

head: Situation
How to adapt
rows: A client who is hard of hearing
Face them in good light so they can see your lips. Speak clearly at a normal pace; do not shout, because it distorts words. Cut background noise and write down the key points.
A deaf client who uses written notes or sign language
Ask how they prefer to communicate. Use clear written notes and sketches, allow time, and check understanding.
A client with poor eyesight
Use large print, read documents aloud, and describe and show where switches and breakers are.
A wheelchair user
Talk to them, not to their companion. Make sure the switches, outlets and controls you fit are within their reach.
An elderly client
Be patient, give time, write down the key points and involve family if the client wishes. Show your ID: many older people worry about strangers.
A visitor from abroad
Use simple English and avoid slang. Explain the 110 V / 220 V, 50 Hz supply.
A client who speaks Patois
Respond naturally and respectfully, and never mock anyone's speech. Make sure written documents are still clear.
Religious or cultural needs
Respect them: for example, no work on the Sabbath or during a prayer meeting, or removing shoes indoors. Plan the work around them.
A client with little money
The same respect. Explain what must be done now for safety and what can wait, and offer stages.

ul: Never make jokes or comments about anyone's background, looks, gender or beliefs, and stop team members who do.
Do not make assumptions, such as speaking only to the man when a couple is deciding together.
A client's choices about their own home are theirs to make, as long as the work is safe and meets the code.

blocks.h: Respect for the client's home and premises

ul: Protect floors and furniture with dust sheets; ask before moving anything.
Remove offcuts, packaging and dust at the end of every day.
No smoking, loud music or bad language on site.
Ask before using a toilet, water or electricity.
Keep gates closed so pets and livestock do not get out.
In a shop, school or office, keep walkways clear and work around opening hours where you can.

blocks.note: Vans, uniforms and behaviour are the first things a client sees. A clean van and a polite team tell the client that the firm takes care; a dirty one tells them the opposite before you have done any work.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **complaint** is a client's statement that they are unhappy with the service. Treat it as a chance: a client whose complaint is handled well often becomes more loyal than one who never had a problem. A client who is ignored tells everyone.

flow: Listen to the whole complaint without interrupting, arguing or making excuses
Thank the client for telling you and apologise for the trouble caused
Ask questions to get the facts, and repeat them back
If there is any danger, make the installation safe at once
Say what you will do and by when, and agree the fix with the client
Pass on (escalate) anything beyond your authority, and tell the client who will contact them and when
Record the complaint in the complaint log
Put it right promptly, done by a competent person
Follow up to check the client is satisfied
Find the cause with the team and change what led to it

blocks.p: Say sorry for the trouble the client has had: 'I'm sorry the power was off so long; I know that cost you a morning's work.' Do not blame a trainee, the supplier, JPS or the client in front of the client. Find the facts first; who was at fault is decided later, calmly.

ul: Stay calm and keep your voice low and steady. Do not take it personally.
Move the conversation somewhere quiet, away from customers or neighbours.
Let them speak. Use their name and show you understand how they feel.
Focus on what can be done now.
If a client shouts at a trainee, step in calmly and take over the conversation.
If you are threatened or abused, end the conversation politely, move away and call your supervisor. Never touch the client.

blocks.h: What you can decide and what you must escalate

blocks.p: **Escalation** means passing a problem to a more senior person who has the authority to deal with it. Never promise what you cannot authorise, and never refuse it either: say who will decide, and by when.

head: Usually the team leader can
Usually passed to the manager
rows: Listen, apologise and record the complaint
Refunds, discounts or compensation for the client's losses
Make the installation safe
Disputes about the bill, and billing errors
Put right poor workmanship on the team's own job
Damage claims, insurance claims and legal threats
Clean up or redo minor finishing
Complaints about a staff member's conduct
Arrange a return visit within the firm's standards
Anything that changes the price or the contract

ul: Date and time received, and who took it
Client's name, site and contact details
The complaint, in the client's words
The facts found and any immediate action, such as making safe
The agreed fix and its date
Anything escalated: to whom, and when the client will hear
The follow-up date and the result
The cause, and what was changed so it does not happen again

blocks.note: Write facts, not opinions. 'Client reports the outlet circuit trips when the kettle is used; checked at 2 p.m.; loose neutral found and remade' helps. 'Client is very difficult' does not.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: If a client complains on social media, the reply is usually made by the manager, following the firm's policy. Reply politely and briefly, do not argue in public, offer to talk privately, and never post the client's details. Then deal with the complaint in the usual way.

Keep asking 'why?' until you reach something the firm can change. **Example:** the shutdown overran → the old supply cable was corroded → nobody checked it on the survey → the survey checklist does not include the supply cable. The fix is to add it to the checklist, warn clients of the risk and book shutdowns with spare time.

The work must be finished, tested and passed, inspected where required, energised by the authorised person, and the area cleaned. Any snags must be cleared. Never hand over in a rush because the client is waiting.

head: Show the client
Hand over
rows: Where the main switch is, and how to switch off in an emergency
How to reset a tripped breaker, and that one which keeps tripping means a fault: call the firm
How to press the TEST button on GFCI outlets and breakers regularly
How to use any new equipment, such as a timer, isolator or changeover switch
Not to overload circuits or use unsafe adaptors
The test certificate or test results
The updated circuit chart (panel schedule)
Drawings of the work, where there are any
The makers' manuals and warranty cards
The firm's warranty, how to contact the firm, and the invoice

blocks.p: Walk the client round, answer questions and ask them to sign that they have received everything. A short meeting like this at the end of a job is called the **handover**.
A **call-back** is a return visit to put right a fault in work the firm has already done. Answer warranty calls within the firm's standard and go and find the cause.

ul: If the fault is in the firm's work, put it right at no charge and apologise.

If the fault is somewhere else, such as the client's own appliance or a JPS supply problem, explain what you found in plain words, show the evidence (for example, your readings) and advise who can fix it.
The firm's policy on charging for visits that find no fault in its work should be explained at the start of the job, not after the visit.
Record every call-back. The number of call-backs per job is one of the clearest measures of the quality of the work.

blocks.p: After every service call, write a short report: what the client reported, what you found, any readings, what you did, the parts used and anything still to do. The office and the next person to visit then start from the facts, not from memory.

A **follow-up** is a call or visit soon after a job, often within about a week, to check that everything works and the client is happy. Ask a few short questions, thank the client and deal at once with any problem raised.

A **service standard** is a written target for a part of the service, so that every client gets the same good service, whoever deals with them. A good standard is **specific, measurable and realistic**, and every member of the team knows it.

head: Part of the service
Example standard
rows: Phone calls
Answered within four rings; messages returned within 4 working hours.
Quotations
Sent within 3 working days of the survey visit.
Arrival
A message the day before with a two-hour arrival window; a call if the team will be late.
Tidiness
Work areas cleaned at the end of each day.
Paperwork
Test results and job cards with the office within one working day of finishing.
Warranty calls
A visit within one working day.
Follow-up
Every client called within 7 days of handover.

blocks.p: 'We reply quickly' is not a standard: nobody can check it. 'Messages are returned within 4 working hours' is.

**Working hours example.** The office is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday, and calls must be returned within 4 working hours. A call comes in at 3:30 p.m. on Friday. Friday has 1½ working hours left, so 2½ hours remain on Monday: the call must be returned by **10:30 a.m. on Monday**.

head: Measure
How to work it out
Example
rows: Satisfaction rate
satisfied clients ÷ clients asked × 100
46 satisfied out of 50 asked: 46 ÷ 50 × 100 = 92%
On-time arrival rate
visits on time ÷ all visits × 100
57 of 60 visits on time = 95%
Call-back rate
call-backs ÷ jobs done × 100
6 call-backs from 150 jobs = 4%
Complaint rate
complaints ÷ jobs done × 100
9 complaints from 300 jobs = 3%
Standard met
times the standard was met ÷ times it applied × 100
Quotations on time: 38 of 40 = 95%

blocks.p: Compare **rates**, not raw numbers, when the amount of work changes. **Example:** last year 15 complaints from 300 jobs is 5%. This year 18 complaints from 450 jobs is 4%. The number went up, but the service improved, because the firm did many more jobs.

ul: Ask every client a few short questions after each job, by phone, message or a printed card: Did we arrive when promised? Did we explain things clearly? Did we leave the place clean? Are you happy with the work? Would you use us again? Leave space for comments.
Record complaints, compliments and call-backs as well.
Thank clients for their feedback, and reply to anyone who raises a problem.

flow: Plan: each month, look for patterns and choose one or two things to improve
Do: agree the change with the team and the manager and put it into practice
Check: watch the next months' figures to see whether it worked
Act: keep the change if it worked, or try something else

blocks.p: **Example.** Feedback shows that clients often did not know when the team would arrive. The team starts messaging each client the day before with a time window. Over the next two months, complaints about arrival times fall.

ul: Brief the team on the standards and explain why each one matters to clients.
Set the example in punctuality, dress, language and tidiness.

If a team member is rude or careless with clients, talk to them **privately** and soon: describe what you saw, explain its effect on the client and the firm, agree what will change, coach them and follow up. Report it if it continues.
Praise good service, in front of the team, and pass on compliments from clients.
Plan the day's service calls by area, so less time is spent travelling and more is left for each client.
Involve the team in finding improvements: they see problems the office does not.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain the difference between internal and external customers, with examples of each in an electrical firm.
I can explain how poor internal service reaches the client, using the service chain.
I can prepare for and run a first visit: greet, ask open questions, listen actively, check the installation, repeat back and record the needs.
I can tell a stated need from an unstated need and suggest something that meets both.
I can explain a technical problem to a client in plain words, with the choices and costs.
I can list what a quotation should contain, including exclusions and GCT on its own line.
I can give dates and prices I can keep, and tell a client early and honestly when a promise must change.
I can refuse an unsafe request politely, explain why, offer a safe choice and record my advice.
I can explain why a generator must never be connected by a cord into an outlet.
I can act honestly about side jobs, gifts and property found on site, and keep clients' keys, codes and details confidential.
I can adapt how I communicate for clients who are hard of hearing, elderly, from abroad or have other needs, while giving everyone the same standard of service.
I can handle a complaint step by step, escalate what is beyond my authority and record it in the complaint log.
I can find the cause of a complaint and suggest a change that stops it happening again.
I can carry out a handover and explain the firm's warranty and call-backs.
I can write a measurable service standard and work out satisfaction, call-back and complaint rates.
I can coach a team member whose service is poor, privately and fairly.

terms: Active listening
Listening carefully, showing you are listening, and repeating back what was said to check you have understood.
Call-back
A return visit to put right a fault in work already done.
Closed question
A question answered with yes, no or one fact.
Complaint
A client's statement that they are unhappy with the service.
Complaint log
The firm's record of each complaint, the facts, the fix, any escalation and the follow-up.
Confidentiality
The duty not to share a client's keys, codes, personal details or private matters.
Escalation
Passing a problem to a more senior person who has the authority to deal with it.
Exclusion
Something a quotation states is not included in the price.
External customer
A client or member of the public outside the firm who pays for or uses its services.
Feedback
Clients' comments on the service, good or bad.
Follow-up
A call or visit soon after a job to check that the client is happy.
Handover
The meeting at the end of a job where the work and documents are explained and passed to the client.
Internal customer
A person inside the firm who relies on your work, such as the stores clerk, estimator or office.
Open question
A question starting with words like what, how or why, which gets the client to explain in their own words.
Quotation
A written offer setting out the work, price, exclusions and terms before the job is agreed.
Service standard
A written, measurable target for part of the service, such as returning calls within 4 working hours.
Unstated need
A need behind the client's request that they do not mention.
Variation
A written, agreed change to the work, with its effect on price and time, signed before the change is made.

c1.title: A home office in Red Hills
c1.text: Latoya Brown, a Level 3 electrician, leads a two-person team for a small contracting firm. She visits Mr Everton Reid, who runs an accounting business from a back bedroom of his house in Red Hills, St Andrew. He says the room 'needs more plugs' and wants a new 220 V air-conditioner in it. Latoya finds that his panel has no spare spaces. JPS outages are common on his road, so he asks her to 'fix up a cord' that plugs his portable generator into the clothes-dryer outlet, the way his neighbour does. He wants all the work done in one day next week, as clients are coming to see him.

c2.title: Missing paperwork at a Montego Bay contractor
c2.text: Rohan Clarke leads one of four installation teams at an electrical contractor in Montego Bay, St James. This month the estimator, Mr Patrick Lewis, has had to send two quotations back because Rohan's survey sheets had no cable route lengths. The stores clerk, Miss Sonia Gordon, says the team sends its material requests as voice notes at 6:30 a.m. and expects them packed by 7. The office says test results for two finished jobs have still not been handed in.

c3.title: A long shutdown at an Old Harbour bakery
c3.text: Andre Watson's team was booked to change the main panel at Mrs Hyacinth Morgan's bakery in Old Harbour, St Catherine, with the power off from 8 a.m. to 10 a.m. on a Tuesday. When the old panel came out, the team found the supply cable from the meter badly corroded. It had to be replaced, which needed a JPS crew to disconnect and reconnect the service, and the power stayed off until 1 p.m. A batch of dough spoiled. Mrs Morgan phones Andre, shouting that she has lost J$85 000 of bread and that the firm must pay her today.

c4.title: A church hall in Christiana
c4.text: Kerry-Ann Thompson leads a team rewiring the hall of a church in Christiana, Manchester. The committee chair, Deacon Lloyd Barnes, has asked that no work be done during the Wednesday evening prayer meeting or on Sundays, which makes the programme a week longer. The keyholder, Mother Pearl Lindo, is 83 and hard of hearing; she opens and locks the hall each day. While stripping out old wiring above the ceiling, a trainee finds an old envelope holding a large amount of cash.

c5.title: A dental clinic in Savanna-la-Mar
c5.text: Marlon Grant's team has installed a sub-panel and new circuits for a dental chair, an air compressor and the surgery lighting at Dr Nadine Wallace's clinic in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. The work has been tested, inspected and energised, and carries the firm's six-month warranty. The firm's standard is to visit within one working day of a warranty call. Three weeks after handover, Dr Wallace phones to say that the compressor's breaker trips most mornings.

questions.q: Which question should Latoya ask first to learn what Mr Reid really needs in the office?
o: Shall we fit standard double outlets, or the type with USB ports?
Would Monday morning suit you for us to start the wiring work?
What do you use in this room, and where do you sit to work?
Is J$20 000 roughly what you were planning to spend on this?
questions.why: An open question gets him to describe how he works, which tells Latoya what equipment there is, where outlets are needed and what loads the circuits must carry. The other questions are closed and settle details before she knows the needs.

questions.q: How should Latoya answer Mr Reid's request for a generator cord into the dryer outlet?
o: Refuse, explain the back-feed danger, and price a proper changeover switch
Make the cord, but warn him in writing to switch off the main breaker each time
Make the cord only if he signs a letter saying he takes full responsibility
Refuse, and advise him instead to buy a generator big enough for the house
questions.why: A cord with a plug on each end has live, exposed pins, and if the main is left on it feeds power back through the meter into JPS lines, where it can kill a line worker. Warnings and signed letters do not remove the danger. A changeover switch, installed and inspected, means the house can never be fed by JPS and the generator at the same time.

questions.q: Mr Reid wants everything done in one day next week. What should Latoya tell him about the timing?
o: Promise one day to keep his business, then deal with the panel on the day
Put the A/C on the new outlet circuit so the whole job fits into a single day
Say nothing about time yet, and decide on the day once the team sees how it goes
Outlets in a day, but the A/C needs board work first; give a date she can keep
questions.why: Promise only what you can keep. A full panel means extra work and perhaps parts on order, so Latoya should explain this now and give a realistic date in writing. A 220 V A/C cannot share a 110 V outlet circuit, and a broken promise costs the client more than an honest date.

questions.q: Which item should Latoya list as an exclusion on the written quotation?
o: Testing the new circuits before they are put into use
Repainting the walls where cables are chased in
The breakers and cable needed for the new circuits
Removing offcuts and dust at the end of each day
questions.why: An exclusion tells the client what he must arrange or pay for separately, such as patching and repainting, so there is no argument later. Testing, materials and cleaning up are part of doing the job properly and are never left out.

questions.q: In this story, which people are Rohan's internal customers?
o: Mr Lewis, Miss Gordon and the office staff
The clients whose quotations were sent back
The electrical inspector and the JPS crews
Only the supervisor who leads the four teams
questions.why: Internal customers are people inside the firm who need something from Rohan's team to do their own work: the estimator needs measurements, the store needs clear requests in time and the office needs test results. Clients, the inspector and JPS are outside the firm.

questions.q: What is the main harm to clients when survey sheets reach the estimator without route lengths?
o: None, since the team will measure the routes again on the first day of work
The stores clerk must then order the cable in several smaller deliveries
Only that the estimator has to stay late to finish his paperwork
Quotes are late or wrong, so the client waits or the price is unfair
questions.why: The estimator prices from the survey. Missing lengths mean guessing, which gives a price too low (the firm loses money) or too high (the firm loses the job), or the sheet goes back and the client waits. Poor internal service ends up as poor service to the client.

questions.q: Which change would best serve Miss Gordon, the stores clerk?
o: Send the voice notes earlier, at about 6:00 a.m. instead of 6:30 a.m.
Let each team member collect what he needs from the shelves himself
Agree a cut-off: written requests by 3 p.m. are packed for 7 a.m. next day
Ask the supervisor to tell her that the teams' needs must always come first
questions.why: A written request with sizes, types, quantities and the job number, sent by an agreed time, lets the store pick and check the order properly. An internal service agreement tells each side what to expect. Helping yourself from the shelves loses track of stock.

questions.q: Why do the missing test results matter to the two clients themselves?
o: They do not, as test results are kept only for the firm's own files
Their certificates and final paperwork are held up until they arrive
The clients will be charged a second time for the testing to be done
Their new breakers cannot be reset until the results are handed in
questions.why: The test results are needed to complete the certificate and the job file, so a client who has paid for safe, certified work is left waiting and chasing the office. Handing in paperwork on time is service to the office and, through it, to the client.

questions.q: What should Andre do first on the phone with Mrs Morgan?
o: Let her finish, show he understands and apologise for the trouble
Explain at once that the corroded cable was not the team's fault
Agree to pay the J$85 000 so that she calms down and stays a client
Tell her he is busy on site and ask her to phone the office instead
questions.why: An upset client first needs to be heard. Interrupting with reasons sounds like an excuse, and Andre has no authority to agree a payment. Listening, showing he understands her loss and apologising for the trouble calms the call so the facts can be dealt with.

questions.q: Mrs Morgan insists the firm pays for the bread. What is the right reply from Andre?
o: Refuse straight away, since the cable was corroded before the team arrived
Promise the firm will pay, as long as she sends him a receipt for the flour
Say it is the manager's decision, and tell her who will call and when
Tell her to claim from JPS, because its crew was the reason for the delay
questions.why: Compensation is a money and contract decision, usually above a team leader's authority. Andre should neither promise nor refuse it: he escalates it, records it, and tells her who will contact her and by when, then makes sure that happens.

questions.q: When the team reviews the complaint, which change would best stop it happening again?
o: Never tell clients how long a shutdown will take, so they cannot complain
Ask shop owners to sign that they accept any losses caused during work
Leave old supply cables in place, even when they are found corroded
Check the supply cable on the survey and allow spare time in shutdowns
questions.why: The cause was a tight two-hour shutdown booked without checking the supply cable. Adding it to the survey checklist, warning clients of the risk and booking shutdowns with spare time, or outside baking hours, deals with the cause. Hiding information or leaving a corroded cable makes things worse.

questions.q: Which entry belongs in the firm's complaint log?
o: Client was very difficult and shouted down the phone at the team leader
Overran 3 h (corroded cable); J$85 000 claim to manager, reply by Thu
The trainee probably took too long to take the old panel off the wall
Complaint dealt with on the phone; nothing more is needed on this one
questions.why: A log entry records facts: what happened, the claim, who it was passed to and when the client will hear. Opinions about the client or guesses about a team member do not help, and a complaint is not closed until it has been followed up.

questions.q: How should Kerry-Ann explain to Mother Lindo which parts of the hall will be without power each day?
o: Speak loudly from across the hall so that she hears every word
Face her in good light, speak clearly and write down the key points
Explain it only to the deacon, as she is too old to need the detail
Give her the full drawings and programme to read when she gets home
questions.why: Many people who are hard of hearing partly lip-read, so face her in good light and speak clearly without shouting, which distorts words. A short written note of the times and areas gives her something to check later. Leaving her out because of her age is disrespectful, and she is the one who opens the hall.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do about the envelope of cash?
o: Leave it where it was found in the ceiling and say nothing about it
Let the trainee keep it, as it was clearly lost many years ago
Count it with a witness and hand it to the deacon against a signature
Take it to the firm's office for safe keeping until the job is finished
questions.why: Anything found on a client's premises belongs to the client. Counting it with a witness, handing it over against a signature and recording it protects the church, the trainee and the firm's good name. Keeping, hiding or removing it would all raise questions of honesty.

questions.q: The deacon's request about Wednesday evenings and Sundays makes the programme longer. What is the best response?
o: Respect it, plan around those times and confirm the dates in writing
Ask the committee to cancel the prayer meeting for the weeks of the work
Work quietly on Sundays anyway, to keep the job on its first programme
Agree, then add a charge for the lost days to the final bill without saying
questions.why: A client's religious and cultural needs are part of what they need from the service. Planning around them and confirming the working days in writing keeps both the promise and the relationship. Any real extra cost is discussed openly, not added as a surprise.

questions.q: At handover, what is most important for Marlon to show Dr Wallace and her receptionist?
o: How to open the sub-panel cover and tighten the terminal screws monthly
How to fit a larger breaker in place of one that keeps on tripping
How to bypass the sub-panel if the dental chair stops during a patient
How to switch off the sub-panel in an emergency and reset a breaker
questions.why: Users need to know how to cut the power quickly in an emergency and how to reset a tripped breaker safely, and to call the firm if it keeps tripping. Opening the panel, changing breakers or bypassing protection is work for an electrician, never for the client.

questions.q: On the warranty visit, Marlon finds the circuit and breaker in order, but the compressor's start capacitor has failed, so the motor draws a very high current when it starts. What should he tell Dr Wallace?
o: Fit a bigger breaker so that the compressor can start, and say nothing more about it
Explain, with the readings, that the compressor is faulty; refer her to its supplier
Tell her that the wiring is not the firm's problem and leave without giving advice
Replace the breaker free of charge, since the clinic's job is still under warranty
questions.why: The warranty covers the firm's work, and here the fault is in the client's equipment. Honest service means explaining what was found in plain words, with the evidence, and pointing her to the equipment supplier. A bigger breaker would leave the cable unprotected, and replacing a healthy breaker fixes nothing.

questions.q: Why should the firm phone Dr Wallace about a week after the compressor is repaired?
o: To remind her that the six-month warranty will soon be coming to an end
To ask her to pay for the visit that found the faulty capacitor
To check the problem is solved and that she is happy with the service
To ask her to agree that the call-back can be left out of the records
questions.why: A follow-up call checks that the problem really is solved and that the client is satisfied, and gives her a chance to raise anything else. It shows care and often turns a problem into loyalty. Call-back records are kept honestly, not edited.

questions.q: Last year a firm had 12 call-backs from 240 jobs. This year it had 15 call-backs from 375 jobs. What happened to its call-back rate?
o: It rose from 12% to 15%
It stayed the same at 5%
It rose by 25%, from 12 to 15
It fell from 5% to 4%
questions.why: A rate compares call-backs with jobs done: 12 ÷ 240 × 100 = 5% and 15 ÷ 375 × 100 = 4%. The number of call-backs rose, but the firm did many more jobs, so the rate improved. Compare rates, not raw counts, when the amount of work changes.

questions.q: Which of these is the best-written service standard for a team?
o: Quotations are sent out to every client as quickly as we can
Quotations are sent within 3 working days of the survey
Clients should be kept happy with our quotes at all times
Staff will try hard to send a quote soon after each visit
questions.why: A good service standard is specific and measurable, so everyone knows the target and the firm can count how often it is met. 'As quickly as we can' or 'try hard' cannot be measured or checked.
